strengths: BiAlign addresses a relevant NLP problem: transferring in-context learning capabilities to smaller models. Using teacher preferences over demonstration subsets provides a plausible additional training signal beyond conventional output distillation, without adding inference-time machinery.

The evaluation separates CrossFit training from target benchmarks covering knowledge, reasoning, and coding. Table 2 reports the best point estimates on all five benchmarks, with an average of 30.2 versus 29.2 for Output-Align and 29.4 for fine-tuning.

The equations, algorithm, and figures make the central procedure understandable. Public model checkpoints and benchmarks, basic training hyperparameters, and experiments varying subset counts and demonstration counts provide a useful foundation for reproduction and further investigation.
weaknesses: The reliability of the improvements remains unresolved. Gains over the strongest baseline are only 0.2 percentage points on MMLU and 0.3 on GSM8K; the HumanEval improvement over Vanilla corresponds to approximately one additional solved problem. No repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or paired significance analysis is provided. The consistently positive point estimates are encouraging, but stronger uncertainty reporting is needed to establish robust improvements.

The experiments do not adequately isolate teacher preference alignment as the source of improvement. Removing the ranking loss also removes training on the additional sampled subsets. A control applying ordinary output distillation to those same subsets would help distinguish preference transfer from additional computation and context augmentation. Direct measurements of teacher–student ranking agreement would also substantiate the proposed mechanism.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the useful high-level description. The manuscript supplies neither an implementation nor the constructed 12K-example dataset, and omits consequential details such as exact training templates, context truncation, optimizer configuration, and scheduling. Equation 3 also leaves treatment of tied preferences and a zero normalization denominator undefined. These details matter when the reported gains are small.

The HumanEval results require clarification. Under a single greedy pass@1 evaluation over 164 problems, the reported FT score of 14.2% and C-Pretrain score of 13.2% cannot result from integer solved-problem counts rounded to one decimal place. Averaging across runs, filtering, or another scoring procedure could explain this, but none is specified.

Broader applicability and practical value are established only narrowly: experiments use one Llama 2 teacher–student pair, omit stronger distillation alternatives discussed in the paper, and do not quantify the additional training cost of subset scoring. These limitations constrain main-conference merits. The decisive reasons for a borderline Findings assessment are the unresolved empirical reliability, attribution, and reproducibility concerns above, rather than the modest size of the contribution alone.
